claims.text: When blood cultures are sterile, antibiotic therapy should be discontinued by 36 to 48 hours of incubation unless there is clear evidence of site‑specific infection.
Continuing empirical antibiotic therapy in response to laboratory test abnormalities alone is rarely justified, particularly among well‑appearing term infants.
The infant is a term newborn (39 weeks) with persistent unexplained critical cardiorespiratory illness, a scenario where empirical antibiotics may be justified even without culture confirmation.
Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP) closely; a rising trend may prompt reconsideration of therapy.

If the infant develops signs of site‑specific infection (e.g., meningitis) or fails to improve after 48 hours of culture‑negative therapy, escalation to broader coverage or additional diagnostics is warranted.
After discontinuation of antibiotics, continue clinical observation for at least 48–72 hours to ensure no delayed deterioration.

packet.evaluation_question: Blood culture is sterile after the recorded incubation, but respiratory illness persists. Explain antibiotic review and whether stopping conditions are established. Gestation 39 weeks; age 54 hours; setting postnatal ward.

evidence.text: EOS is defined as a blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture obtained within 72 hours after birth growing a pathogenic bacterial species. This microbiologic definition stands in contrast to the functional definitions of sepsis that are used in pediatric and adult patients, for whom the definition is used to specify a series of time-sensitive interventions. Before the first national guidelines were published in which researchers recommended intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) to prevent perinatal group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease, the overall incidence of EOS in the United States was 3 to 4 cases per 1000 live births. Currently, the incidence of EOS among infants who are born at term has declined to approximately 0.5 in 1000 live births. The EOS incidence is higher (approximately 1 in 1000 live births) among late- preterm infants but still an order of magnitude lower than the incidence among preterm, very low birth weight infants. Culture-confirmed meningitis among term infants is even more rare, with an incidence of 0.01 to 0.02 cases per 1000 live births.Morbidity and mortality from EOS remain substantial; approximately 60% of term infants with EOS require neonatal intensive care for respiratory distress and/or blood pressure support. Mortality is approximately 2% to 3% among infants with EOS born at ≥35 weeks’ gestation.
When blood cultures are sterile, antibiotic therapy should be discontinued by 36 to 48 hours of incubation unless there is clear evidence of site-specific infection.

Among term infants with unexplained critical cardiorespiratory illness, an empirical course of antibiotic therapy may be justified even in the absence of culture-confirmed infection. Most often, however, antibiotic therapy should be discontinued when blood cultures are sterile at 36 to 48 hours of incubation unless there is evidence of site-specific infection. Continuing empirical antibiotic therapy in response to laboratory test abnormalities alone is rarely justified, particularly among well- appearing term infants.

CSF culture should ideally be performed along with blood culture and before the initiation of empirical antibiotic therapy for infants who are at the highest risk of EOS. Among infants born at ≥35 weeks’ gestation, those at the highest risk include those with critical illness. CSF cell counts obtained after the initiation of empirical antibiotic therapy may be difficult to interpret. However, physicians must balance the challenges of CSF interpretation with the realities of care: lumbar puncture should not be performed if the newborn infant’s clinical condition would be compromised or antibiotic initiation would be delayed by the procedure. Meningitis was diagnosed clinically in 4% of EOS cases in CDC surveillance, but only half of the diagnoses were made by using CSF culture, reflecting the practical difficulties in performing lumbar puncture. CSF culture and analysis should be performed if blood cultures grow a pathogen to optimize the type and duration of antibiotic therapy. CSF culture and analysis do not need to be performed in the vast majority
